title: Lecture #43: Java Exception Handling from Scratch
topics: Exception propagation through a chain of methods

questions.question: The notes split runtime "problems" into Exceptions and Errors. Which statement matches that distinction?
options: Exceptions are detected at compile time, while Errors happen only at runtime

An Exception is a recoverable, handleable abnormal condition (wrong input, missing file, divide by zero), while an Error such as `OutOfMemoryError` or `StackOverflowError` is a serious JVM-level problem the program normally should not try to handle
Errors are thrown by your own code, while Exceptions are thrown only by the JVM
An Exception is a plain message string, while an Error is an object
questions.explanation: Exceptions are abnormal but recoverable conditions that occur during execution, and the program can catch them and continue. Errors such as `OutOfMemoryError` or `StackOverflowError` signal problems in the runtime environment that application code usually cannot fix. Both are objects; the notes label each as an "Object", so neither is just a string.

questions.question: What happens when this program runs?
options: It prints "Step 1" and then "Step 2"; the JVM skips the bad line
It prints "Step 1", then 0, then "Step 2"
It does not compile, because the compiler detects the division by zero
It prints "Step 1", then the `ArithmeticException: / by zero` stack trace; "Step 2" is never printed
questions.explanation: With no handler, the JVM creates `new ArithmeticException("/ by zero")`, and the default exception handler prints the exception and stack trace and ends the program. Control never reaches the "Step 2" line, so the JVM does not skip the bad line and carry on. `b` is a variable, so the compiler cannot flag anything here.

questions.question: This is the lecture's Demo3 (a `try` with `finally` but no `catch`). What is the behaviour?
options: It prints "Step 1", "Heyyyy", "Step 2", because `finally` handles the exception
It prints "Step 1", then the stack trace; "Heyyyy" is skipped because there is no catch
It prints "Step 1" and "Heyyyy", then the `ArithmeticException` stack trace; "Step 2" is never printed
It does not compile, because every `try` must have at least one `catch`
questions.explanation: `finally` always runs, but it does not handle the exception. After printing "Heyyyy", the ArithmeticException keeps propagating out of `main`, and the default handler terminates the program. `try` with only `finally` is legal Java; a `try` just needs a `catch` or a `finally` (or to be try-with-resources).

questions.question: A batch job processes 1,000 rows in a `for` loop. Row 37 triggers an `ArithmeticException`, and the whole job stops, so rows 38-1000 are never processed. The goal from the notes is "when an exception occurs, don't crash; handle it and continue." Where should the try-catch go?
options: Inside the loop, around the processing of a single row, so a failure is reported for that row and the loop moves on to the next one
Around the entire `for` loop, so the job catches the exception once and then resumes from row 38
In a `finally` block after the loop, so that skipped rows get processed later
Around the `main` method declaration, so the JVM retries the failed row
questions.explanation: Once an exception leaves the try block, control jumps to the catch and never returns to the point of the throw. A try around the whole loop therefore ends the loop at row 37. Putting the try-catch inside the loop body contains each failure to its own row. Java has no automatic resume or retry.

questions.question: In Demo2, `main()` calls `methodA()`, which calls `methodB()`, which computes `a / b` with `b = 0`, and nobody has a try-catch. What exactly does the JVM do?
options: It returns 0 from `methodB`, logs a warning and lets `main` continue

It creates an `ArithmeticException` object in `methodB` and looks back up the call stack (methodB, methodA, main) for a matching handler; finding none, the default exception handler prints the exception with its stack trace and terminates the thread
It restarts `methodB` with `b` reset to 1, so the division can succeed
It terminates the program immediately without creating any exception object or printing anything
questions.explanation: When nothing handles the exception, the JVM decides everything: it builds an exception object describing the problem, unwinds the call stack frame by frame looking for a handler, and if none exists, the default handler prints the stack trace and ends the thread (here the main thread, so the program ends). The detailed trace is what makes debugging possible, which is why "nothing printed" is wrong.

questions.question: When Demo2 crashes, which method appears on the first "at ..." line (the top frame) of the printed stack trace?
options: `Demo2.main`, because the program started there
`Demo2.methodA`, because it passed the bad argument along
`java.lang.ArithmeticException.<init>`, because the constructor runs first
`Demo2.methodB`, because that is where the exception was thrown; `methodA` and then `main` appear below it
questions.explanation: A stack trace lists frames from the most recent call (where the exception occurred) down to the entry point. So the order is methodB, then methodA, then main, mirroring the call-stack picture in the notes. `main` is at the bottom, not the top.

questions.question: Your method opens a file, reads it and parses numbers, and parsing may throw. Whether parsing succeeds, fails and is caught, or fails and is not caught, the file must be closed and a "done" log line written. Where does that code belong?
options: In a `finally` block, because it runs whether the try block completes normally or exits with an exception
At the end of the `try` block, because the try block always runs to completion
In the `catch` block only, because cleanup is needed only when something goes wrong
After the whole try-catch statement, because code there always runs even if an exception escapes
questions.explanation: The code comments in the lecture list exactly this as `finally`'s job: cleanup, closing resources and logging. The end of the try block is skipped when an exception occurs. Code after the try statement does not run if an uncaught exception escapes, as Demo3's missing "Step 2" shows.

questions.topic: Exception propagation through a chain of methods
questions.question: This time the handler is in `methodA`, not where the exception happens. What is the output?
options:
Start
Caught in A: / by zero
B done
A done
End

Start
Caught in A: / by zero
A after B
A done
End

Start
Caught in A: / by zero
A done
End

Start
Caught in A: / by zero
A done
questions.explanation: The exception aborts `methodB` immediately, so "B done" never prints. It propagates to `methodA`, where the rest of the try block ("A after B") is skipped and the catch runs. After the catch, normal flow resumes: "A done" prints and control returns to `main`, which prints "End".

questions.question: A teammate wraps `System.out.println(a / b);` in `try { ... } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("handled"); } finally { System.out.println("cleanup"); }` and believes the program is now crash-proof. What actually happens when `b` is 0?
options: It prints "handled" and "cleanup", because any catch block handles any exception
It prints "cleanup", and then the ArithmeticException propagates and crashes the program, because the catch only matches `NullPointerException`
It prints only "handled", because `finally` is skipped once a catch block exists
It does not compile, because an `ArithmeticException` can only be caught by a catch clause for that exact type
questions.explanation: A catch block runs only if the thrown exception's type matches its parameter type. `ArithmeticException` is not a `NullPointerException`, so the handler is skipped. `finally` still runs ("cleanup"), and then the exception continues up the stack to the default handler. The code compiles fine; there is simply no matching handler.

questions.question: The lecture's classic exception is `int a = 5, b = 0; a / b` throwing `ArithmeticException("/ by zero")`. If the same values are stored in `double x = 5, y = 0;`, what does `x / y` do, and why?
options: It evaluates to `Infinity` without throwing, because floating-point arithmetic (IEEE 754) has a representation for infinity, whereas `int` has none, so integer division by zero must throw
It also throws `ArithmeticException("/ by zero")`, because any division by zero is illegal in Java
It evaluates to 0.0, because the JVM silently replaces invalid double results with zero
It throws `ArithmeticException`, but only when assertions are enabled with `-ea`
questions.explanation: Java's floating-point types follow IEEE 754, so 5.0 / 0.0 is `Infinity` (and 0.0 / 0.0 is `NaN`), and no exception is created. Integer types have no infinity value, so the JVM signals the abnormal condition by creating an ArithmeticException. Assuming that every division by zero throws is a common misconception.
